text: I woke to cold stone and a dim fire. The ash smells like old bread. My armor rattles when I move. I sat, lit the candle, and tried to remember who I was. I found a rusted dagger and a half‑filled ink bottle on the desk. I will write down what I do, one day at a time.

I finished the inventory list and set the candle stub aside. The ragged oak scrap I found in the corner looks good for a frame, so I measured it with my thumb. The fire crackled louder when I talked to it about my plans – it seemed to nod. I noticed a loose stone near the hearth that might be a clue to a missing support. My mind drifted to the roof gap; the wind whistles through it, reminding me the stone can’t be trusted forever. I feel mostly content, a little curious about the window glass I might restore. I’ll spend the next two hours tightening what I can and gathering more bits.

I shifted the stones on the doorway again. The pile is a third cleared now, but a stubborn slab still clings. The fire kept me company, humming like a coworker. I found a piece of cracked glass in the dust and tucked it into my pocket for later. The candle flickered low, so I trimmed the wick and set it back. My mind drifted to the roof; the wind whistles through the gap. I feel warm and fairly rested, a bit amused by the stone’s resistance. My thoughts are on repair and a new craft idea for a small tool rack. I will spend the next two hours tightening the doorway, checking the hearth stones, and sketching the rack design.

I pried another slab loose and wedged it against the cleared stones. The gap narrowed enough to see a sliver of courtyard light. A second shard of glass slipped from my pocket and cracked on the floor; I set it aside for later use.

I cleared the last slab from the doorway and pushed it aside. Light from the courtyard slipped in, lighting the dust. A shard of glass I’d pocketed clinked against the stone when I stepped back. The fire popped, as if approving the work.

I nudged a loose stone into place on the hearth. The mortar felt gritty under my thumb. The fire seemed a bit steadier after that, but the gap still lets cold in. I set the broken brick aside for later and noted the pattern of the cracks.

I tightened the hearth stones again and the fire steadied, which was nice. The lantern upgrade sits on the table, but the oil tank leaks a bit when I tilt it. I tried to fit a new piece of wood into the window frame; the wood warped and the joint slipped. I put the broken brick aside and marked the crack pattern for later. The fire complained when I knocked a glass shard out of my pocket. I think I need a better grip for the next piece.

I finally got the window frame back together. The wood still wants to bow, so I set it aside. The glass shards in my pocket are still whole, but I have no idea what to do with them yet. The fire kept its usual steady burn.

I lay on the bedroll until the fire's heat stopped feeling like a drill sergeant. My arms stopped aching, but the stone still feels like it’s waiting for me to finish it. I noticed the lantern oil still drips when I tilt it, so I’ll have to patch that later.
I fitted the new oil seal onto the bottle and gave it a test tilt. The oil still finds a way out, like a leaky gossip. I’ll have to sand the edge a bit more before it stops spilling.

I kept at the stair, wedging a new slab where the old one cracked. The stone slipped a bit, so I tapped it back with the hammer. The gap still shows a thin line of dust. I think the next piece will need a tighter fit, otherwise the whole thing will wobble when I climb.

I wedged the next stone on the stair and hammered it until it sat flush. The slab shifted a bit when I pressed my foot, so I sanded the edge a little more. The hammer slipped once, bruising my thumb, but the gap is tighter now.

I finally locked the last stone on the stair. The hammer slipped once and left a bruise on my thumb, but the slab now sits flush. The fire seemed a bit too eager for a break, so I gave it a quick poke. The stair feels solid enough to trust for a climb up to the tower.

I added a new layer of mortar to the east wall and it set faster than I expected. The mix was a bit gritty, so I brushed off the excess before it hardened. I realized I used the same stone for the corner as I did for the stair, which might cause a color clash later. The fire crackled louder when I leaned on the workbench, almost like it wanted a break.
I slept on the bedroll until the fire dimmed. Woke feeling the stone still cold under my back, but my thumb stopped throbbing.

I added another course of mortar to the east wall. The mix felt gritty, so I scraped the excess before it set. The fire kept nudging me, asking when I’d finish. I counted the steps on the broken stair again, just for habit. The stone still holds the weight, but I wonder if the roof will ever close.
I set the first stones for the forge today. The mortar smelled of dust and wet stone. My thumb still throbbed from the stair work. The fire kept nudging me about the roof.

I added another layer of bricks to the forge wall. The mortar set faster than I hoped. The fire flickered as I leaned on the anvil, and a stray spark landed on a scrap of cloth. I brushed it off and kept working. The east wall still needs more work, but the forge feels steadier now.

The forge finally stands solid. I tightened the last bolts on the bellows and checked the chimney for cracks. The anvil settled into place without a wobble, which surprised me. While cleaning the workbench I found a shard of glass I hadn't noticed before; it fit nicely in the pocket I keep for broken pieces. I tested the lantern with fresh oil; the light held steady. The roof gap still lets a cold draft in, but the heat from the forge keeps the floor warm enough to sit a while. I noted the mortar on the east wall looks darker where I mixed extra sand today.

I mixed a fresh batch of mortar and laid the last course on the east wall. The mix held better this time, no excess to scrape. A loose stone slipped off the trowel and hit my boot; I muttered about the stone's timing. The wall looks steady enough for now.

I tightened a few more boards over the roof gap. One board warped when I lifted it, so I swapped it for a fresher piece from the stash. The new board fits better, but the gap still lets a cold draft in. I noted the spot where the wind whistles the most.
I cut a new timber for the woodshed roof and nailed it in place. The piece fit without a gap, which surprised me. The fire kept nudging me about the next board.

I tightened the last brace on the woodshed lean‑to and checked the roof joints. One board cracked when I leaned on it, so I swapped it for a fresh piece from the stash. The new board sits tight, no wobble. The fire flickered a warning, but I ignored it for now.
I slipped a fresh plank into the roof gap and the mortar set faster than expected. The fire kept nudging me about the next spot, but I ignored it. The new board holds.

I added another board to the roof gap and the mortar held. The new piece sits tight, but a thin crack appeared in the adjacent stone. I muttered that the stone must be on a coffee break. The fire stayed quiet while I checked the fit.

I swapped the warped plank on the roof with a fresh cut from the stash. The new piece sits snug, and the mortar hardened faster than I expected. A tiny fissure opened in the stone beside it, so I marked it for later. The fire was steady, no complaints.

I closed the last gap in the roof just before dusk. The board fits tight, no wind sneaks in. The fire stayed warm while I tightened the bolts. After that I turned to the glasshouse. I placed three salvaged panes on the potting bench, sealed the joints, and tested the heat. The structure feels stable, though I still need a fourth pane. My hands are sore and the lantern oil is low. I counted the steps up the broken stair twice, just to be sure. The overcast sky presses against the open tiles, but the keep feels a bit safer now.

I finished the glasshouse today. The seedlings are pushing up, a little green against the stone. One of the roof stones near the new board has a hairline crack I hadn't seen before. The fire kept to itself while I worked, no complaints. I noted the crack for later and stepped back to admire the rows of pots.
I cut a new timber beam for the bathhouse floor and fit it. The joint squeaked a bit, so I added a shim. Not much else moved today.
I patched the east wall and the hall feels solid again. While checking the doorway I found a loose stone that kept wobbling when I stepped on it. Guess the stone still needs its coffee break.

I tried to tighten the new bathhouse beam again. The shim slipped a bit, so I added another thin slice. The wood creaked louder than usual, like it was complaining about the rain. I noted the extra slice in the plan and set the hammer aside for a moment.

I ran the stability test on the bathhouse floor. The joint held, no wobble. The extra shim stays put. I marked the result in the plan and set the page aside. The rain keeps pounding, but the wood seems content for now.

I opened the Bathhouse Builder page and saw the new verification field. The checkbox was unchecked, so I clicked it to mark a pass. The page saved without error. The rain drummed louder on the roof while I worked.

I opened the Bathhouse Builder again and saw the verification box already ticked. I added a short note about the extra shim and saved. The rain kept tapping, but the page held steady. No new bugs this round.

I finally pushed the new summary panel live. The total shim count shows up at the top and updates as I add rows. While testing, I noticed the reset button clears everything, even the totals, which is fine for a fresh start but a bit harsh if I forget to save. I added a short tooltip to warn about that. The code looks cleaner now, no stray brackets. I tried counting the stones in the courtyard wall while the rain hammered the roof. One stone was oddly larger than the rest; I put it in my pocket for later. The fire kept its quiet hum, no complaints this time.

I tightened the new support beam for the bathhouse. The joint squeaked, so I wedged another thin strip. The strip stayed, no wobble. I sketched a quick note about adding an export button for the shim list. The rain still taps the roof.

I cleared some old glass shards from the glasshouse floor and put them in my pocket. The seedlings looked fine, but a stray sprout knocked over a pot. I tightened the pot's support and noted the break. The fire kept its steady hum while I worked.

The bathhouse is finally up. I ran a quick soak and the water held steady, no leaks. I wiped the stone and noted the temperature is a nice rise. The lantern on the shelf still flickers, but the new beams feel solid. I logged the work in my notebook.

I fitted the new lantern upgrade onto the table and gave it a test run. The battery holds charge and the handle folds smooth. I noticed a tiny wobble when I lifted it, tightened the screw and it steadied. The light is brighter, and the upgrade feels solid enough for daily use.

label: Stone Counting
text: I cleared the forge floor and sorted the leftover bolts. Found a dented piece of metal and set it aside for later. The fire kept its steady hum while I measured a new plank with my thumb. Noticed a loose stone by the doorway; tapped it back into place.
